rules.message: Network call made structurally inside a for/for-of/for-in/while/do-while statement or an Array forEach/map/filter/reduce callback — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the call's line falls within a loop statement's span, or within an array-iteration callback's own span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — so it fires one request per iteration, the HTTP analogue of N+1 (rate-limit / serial-latency risk). Batch via a bulk endpoint, or gather inputs and issue one request (or a bounded Promise.all). A file with no projected loop spans is silently skipped by this rule — for the `.ts`/`.tsx` files this rule scans, that realistically means a degraded parse (oversized file or syntax failure), the same graceful-degrade policy method-scan already applies to missing symbol spans.

TypeORM's `eager: true` relation option (typically on `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToOne`/`@OneToOne`/`@ManyToMany`/`@JoinTable` option objects — the matcher fires on any `eager: true` line in a file with TypeORM/Sequelize signals, a deliberate heuristic), or Sequelize's `include: [{ all: true }]` — an entity-level eager-load declaration that makes EVERY finder/query of this entity join the association, whether or not that particular caller needs it: the query-time opposite of N+1, over-fetching on every read instead of under-fetching per iteration. Default relations to lazy and opt in per query instead — TypeORM's `relations: [...]`/`relations: { ... }` on the specific `find`/`findOne` call, or Sequelize's own `include: [...]` at the call site — so only the queries that actually use the association pay for the join. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a small lookup table genuinely read together on every access) with `// zzop-eager-relation-declared-ok`.

An explicit `fetch = FetchType.EAGER` on a JPA/Hibernate mapping annotation (`@OneToMany`/`@ManyToOne`/`@OneToOne`/`@ManyToMany`/`@ElementCollection` — the matcher fires on the `fetch = FetchType.EAGER` attribute itself, whichever annotation carries it) forces every finder/query of the owning entity to join and load that association, whether or not the caller needs it — most expensive on `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToMany` collections, where it can pull an unbounded child set on every parent read. Prefer `FetchType.LAZY` and fetch the association explicitly per query that needs it (a JPQL `JOIN FETCH`, an entity graph, or a dedicated projection). Disclosure: this rule only catches the EXPLICIT declaration above — `@ManyToOne`/`@OneToOne` default to EAGER in the JPA spec with no `fetch` attribute at all, so a clean scan here is not proof the entity has no eager-loading cost.

A SQLAlchemy DECLARATION-level eager loader strategy — `lazy` set to `joined`, `subquery`, `selectin` or `immediate` on a `relationship(...)`/`backref(...)`, the legacy `lazy=False` synonym for `joined`, or the same key written as a string inside a SQLModel `sa_relationship_kwargs` dict — makes EVERY query that loads the owning entity also load this association, whether or not that particular caller needs it: the query-time opposite of N+1, over-fetching on every read instead of under-fetching per iteration, and on a collection relationship it can pull an unbounded child set on every parent read. Leave the relationship at SQLAlchemy's lazy default and opt in per query instead — `joinedload(`, `selectinload(` or `subqueryload(` on the specific query that needs the association (or a `raiseload(` default, which turns a forgotten opt-in into a loud error instead of a silent join) — so only the queries that actually use the association pay for it. Three precision limits, stated rather than left to be discovered. (1) The gate is FILE-level: a `sqlalchemy`/`sqlmodel` mention anywhere in the file admits it and the line pattern is the bare `lazy` keyword argument, so a `lazy` entry in an unrelated dict in the same file also fires — the same deliberate heuristic `eager-relation-declared` documents for TypeORM. (2) A whole-line `#` comment is excluded, but an occurrence in a TRAILING `#` comment on a code line is not. (3) Its POSITIVE behavior rests on unit fixtures alone. The Python trees this rule has actually been run against contain no instance of the shape at all — their ORM relationship declarations sit at the lazy default — so it is measured to stay silent on correct code and measured not at all for recall; read a first run's count as candidates to review, not as a calibrated rate. Suppression, and the one place its spelling is not the usual one: the derived marker is `zzop-sqlalchemy-eager-relationship-ok`, but the DSL line-scan interpreter honors a marker only behind a `//` comment leader, which Python has no equivalent of — write `# // zzop-sqlalchemy-eager-relationship-ok` on the declaration's own line or the line directly above it.
